title: I/O methods and multiprocessors
kicker: ENCT 303 · Computer Organization and Architecture · Chapters 7–8
subtitle: Three ways to talk to a device, and how many processors are connected and kept in agreement.

sections.title: Programmed I/O
sections.body: With programmed I/O the CPU issues a command and then polls the device’s status register until it is ready, then moves the data itself. It is simple but wastes the CPU: a keyboard polled at full speed spends virtually all its time looking at nothing.

choices.text: The CPU busy-waits and does no useful work.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Polling occupies the processor for the whole device delay.

figures.caption: Figure 7.1.1 — programmed I/O
figures.note: The repeated polls are wasted cycles.
figures.script:
diagram("mode: sequence
[CPU] as c
[I/O module] as m
c -> m : command (read)
m --> c : status: busy
c -> m : poll status
m --> c : status: busy
c -> m : poll status
m --> c : status: ready + data");

sections.title: Interrupt-driven I/O
sections.body: The CPU starts the operation and goes on running other instructions. When the device is ready it raises an interrupt; the CPU finishes its current instruction, saves state, runs a service routine that moves the word, and returns. Efficiency is much better, but every word still costs an interrupt — too expensive for disks.

choices.text: The CPU is free during the device’s delay.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It is only interrupted when the device is ready.

figures.caption: Figure 7.2.1 — interrupt-driven I/O
figures.script:
diagram("mode: sequence
[CPU] as c
[I/O module] as m
c -> m : command (read)
c -> c : run other instructions
m --> c : interrupt: data ready
c -> m : read data word
c -> c : resume program");

sections.title: Direct memory access
sections.body: A DMA controller is given the memory address, the count and the direction, then transfers the whole block between device and memory by itself, stealing bus cycles ("cycle stealing") from the CPU, and interrupts once at the end. One interrupt per block instead of one per word.

worked.why: Transfer a 4 KB block from a device that gives one 4-byte word per transfer.
Interrupt-driven: one interrupt per word. DMA: one interrupt per block.

questions.prompt: How many interrupts does a DMA block transfer cause?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The controller handles every word itself.

figures.caption: Figure 7.3.1 — a DMA transfer
figures.note: The CPU only starts and finishes the transfer.
figures.script:
diagram("mode: sequence
[CPU] as c
[DMA controller] as d
[Memory] as m
[Disk] as k
c -> d : address, count, direction
d -> k : request block
k --> d : data words
d -> m : write words (cycle stealing)
d --> c : one interrupt at the end");

sections.title: Channels and interfaces
sections.body: An I/O channel is a small processor that runs its own I/O program, freeing the CPU further (mainframes); a front-end processor does the same for communications. External interfaces are point-to-point (USB, SATA) or multipoint buses (SCSI): serial links are replacing wide parallel ones because they scale in speed.

questions.prompt: An I/O channel differs from a DMA controller because…

choices.text: It executes its own I/O instructions rather than just moving one block.

sections.title: Multiprocessors and interconnection
sections.body: A tightly-coupled multiprocessor shares memory. Processors are joined by a time-shared common bus (cheap, one at a time), multiport memory, a crossbar switch (any processor to any memory, n² crosspoints), a multistage network (log₂ n stages of small switches) or a hypercube (n = 2ᵈ nodes, each with d neighbours). Arbitration decides who wins a contested resource.

worked.why: Crossbar for 8 processors and 8 memories needs 8 × 8 crosspoints. An omega network needs (n/2) log₂ n 2×2 switches.

questions.prompt: How many neighbours does each node of a 4-dimensional hypercube have?

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: That is the number of nodes.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: In a d-dimensional hypercube every node links to d others, one per bit that can flip.

figures.caption: Figure 8.1.1 — a common bus
figures.note: Cheap, but only one transfer at a time.
figures.script:
diagram("direction: right
group "Common bus" { a1, a2, abus }
[P1] as a1 #blue
[P2] as a2 #blue
[Shared bus] as abus #amber
[Memory] as m #mint
a1 -> abus
a2 -> abus
abus -> m");

problems.prompt: A multi-stage omega network connects 16 processors to 16 memories using 2×2 switches. How many stages and how many switches?
problems.answer: Stages = log₂16 = 4; each stage has 16/2 = 8 switches → 32 switches (versus 256 crosspoints for a crossbar).

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Polling wastes CPU; interrupts free it; DMA moves whole blocks with one interrupt.
  • Interconnect choice trades cost against simultaneous transfers.
